sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte latin de zoo75/1l.xml (edition Carmody 1939, Physiologus Latinus, versio B), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. 33 chapitres correspondant exactement au decoupage du temoin latin (memes xml:id).

div.head: The Lion
div.p: Jacob, blessing his son Judah, said: 'Judah's whelp is a lion's cub, my own offspring -- who shall rouse him?'
The Physiologus says the lion has three natural properties.

The first: it walks in the mountains, and if it happens that hunters seek it, the hunter's scent reaches it; and with its tail it covers its tracks behind it wherever it goes, so that no hunter, following its tracks, may find its lair and capture it.

So too our Savior -- the spiritual lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of Jesse, the son of David -- sent by the Father above, covered the tracks of his divinity from those with understanding, and became, with the angels, an angel; with the archangels, an archangel; with the thrones, a throne; with the powers, a power -- until he descended into the womb of the virgin, and saved mankind which had gone astray. And this being unknown, as he ascended to the Father, the angels above said to those ascending with the Lord: 'Who is this king of glory?' And they answered: 'The Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory.'
The second nature of the lion: when it sleeps, its eyes keep watch, for they are open.

As the bridegroom testifies in the Song of Songs, saying: 'I sleep, but my heart watches.' For indeed my Lord, sleeping bodily on the cross and buried, kept his divinity watchful: 'Behold, he who keeps Israel shall not slumber nor sleep.'
The third nature: when the lioness gives birth to her cub, she bears it dead, and guards it for three days, until its father, coming on the third day, breathes upon its face and brings it to life.
So the almighty Father raised our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, from the dead on the third day, as Jacob said: 'He shall lie down like a lion, and like a lion's cub -- who shall rouse him?'

div.head: The Antelope
div.p: There is an animal exceedingly fierce, so that not even the hunter can approach it. It has long horns shaped like a saw, so that it can even cut down tall and great trees and bring them to the ground. When it grows thirsty, it comes to the great river Euphrates and drinks; and there is there a bush called in Greek 'herecine,' having slender and long shoots; coming to it, the animal begins to play with its horns against the herecine, and while playing, entangles its horns in its shoots. When, after long struggling, it cannot free itself, it cries out with a great voice; and the hunter, hearing its voice, comes and kills it.

So too you, man of God, who strive to be sober and chaste and to live spiritually -- whose two horns are the two Testaments, by which you can cut away and remove from yourself all bodily vices, that is, adultery, fornication, avarice, envy, pride, murder, slander, drunkenness, luxury, and all the pomp of this world -- then the angels and all the powers of the heavens rejoice with you. Beware then, man of God, of drunkenness, lest you be entangled in luxury and pleasure, and be slain by the devil: for wine and women make men apostatize from God.

div.head: The Fire-Stones
div.p: There are fire-bearing stones on a certain mountain of the East, which in Greek are called 'terobolem,' male and female. When they are far from one another, no fire is kindled in them; but when by chance the female draws near the male, at once fire is kindled in them, so that all things around that mountain burn.

Whence you too, men of God who lead this life, keep yourselves far from women, lest, when you draw near to one another, that twin fire be kindled in you, and consume the good things Christ has bestowed upon you. For there are angels of Satan who always assail the righteous -- not only holy men but also chaste women; indeed both Samson and Joseph were tempted through women, one conquered, the other was conquered; Eve and Susanna were tempted, the one conquered, the other was overcome.

The heart must therefore be guarded, and admonished in every way by the divine precepts; for the love of women, whose sin began from the beginning -- that is, from Adam even until now -- rages on among the children of disobedience.

div.head: The Saw-Fish
div.p: There is a sea-monster called the saw-fish, having immense wings. When it sees a ship sailing on the deep, it raises its wings and strives to sail alongside the ship. But when it has raced against the ship for thirty or forty furlongs, unable to bear the labor, it grows faint, and, lowering its wings, draws them back to itself; and the waves of the sea, now that it is weary, carry it back to its former place in the deep.

The sea bears the likeness of this present age; the ships bear the likeness of the righteous, who without shipwreck of faith have passed safely through the midst of the storms and tempests of this world, and have overcome the deadly waves, that is, the opposing powers of this age. The saw-fish, however -- that monster which could not sail on with the ships -- bears the likeness of those who began indeed to remain in good works, but afterward, not persevering in them, were overcome by covetousness, pride, drunkenness, luxury, and various kinds of vices, which submerge them, like the surging waves of the sea, down to the depths: but he who perseveres to the end shall be saved.

div.head: The Caladrius
div.p: There is a bird called the caladrius; of it is written in Deuteronomy: it is not to be eaten. The Physiologus says of it that it is entirely white, having no black part; its inward waste cures dimness of the eyes. It is found in the courts of kings. If anyone is afflicted with sickness, it is known through this caladrius whether he will live or die: if the man's illness is unto death, as soon as it sees the sick man the caladrius turns its face away from him and withdraws, and all know that he is going to die; but if his illness does not reach unto death, the caladrius fixes its gaze upon his face, and takes all his infirmities into itself, and flies up into the sun's air, and burns away his infirmities, and scatters them, and the sick man is healed.

The caladrius, then, has taken on the person of our Savior: our Lord is entirely white, having no blackness in him; as he himself testified: 'The prince of this world comes, and finds nothing in me,' he who committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth. Coming down from his lofty heavens to the ailing people of the Jews, he turned his face from them because of their unbelief; he turned to us the Gentiles, taking away our infirmities; and, bearing our sins, was lifted up on the wood of the cross. For ascending on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men. Indeed, those who did not believe did not receive him; but as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name.

But perhaps you say the caladrius is unclean according to the law: this is true; but the serpent too is unclean, and John testifies of it, saying: 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up'; and elsewhere it is called more prudent than all the beasts. Likewise the lion and the eagle are unclean, yet the one is king of the wild beasts, the other of the birds; according to their kingship, then, they are likened to Christ, but according to their rapacity, to the devil. And there are many other things among created beings that carry a double meaning; some indeed are praiseworthy, others blameworthy -- and the difference lies either in their habits, or in the distinction of their nature.

div.head: The Pelican
div.p: David says in the hundred and first psalm: 'I have become like the pelican of the wilderness.'

The Physiologus says of the pelican that it is exceedingly fond of its young; but when it has brought forth offspring and they begin to grow, they strike their parents in the face; and the parents strike them back and kill them. But on the third day their mother, striking her own side, opens her flank, and leans over her chicks, and pours out her blood upon the bodies of her dead young; and so by her own blood she raises them from death.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ says through the prophet Isaiah: 'I have begotten sons and exalted them, but they have despised me.' The author and founder of all creation, almighty God, begot us; and when we were not, he made us to be; but we, on the contrary, struck him in the face, serving the creature in his sight rather than the Creator. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ ascended to the height of the cross, and, his side having been struck, there came forth blood and water for our salvation and eternal life. For the water is the grace of baptism, and his blood the cup of the new and eternal covenant; which, taking into his holy hands, giving thanks, he blessed, and gave to us to drink unto the remission of sins and life everlasting.

div.head: The Night-Raven
div.p: Of the night-raven, David says in the same psalm: 'I have become like a night-raven in a ruined house.'
The night-raven is an unclean bird, and loves darkness more than light.

This bird bears the likeness of the people of the Jews, who, when our Lord and Savior came to save them, drove him away from themselves, saying: 'We have no king but Caesar; who this man is, we do not know.' Therefore they loved darkness more than light: then the Lord turned to us the Gentiles, and enlightened us, who were sitting in darkness and in the region of the shadow of death; and in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen for us. Of this people the Savior says through the prophet: 'A people whom I did not know has served me'; and elsewhere: 'I will call those not my people, my people, and her not beloved, my beloved.' Of that people of the Jews who loved darkness more than light, the Lord says in the psalm: 'The sons of strangers have lied to me, the sons of strangers have grown old, and have limped away from their paths.'

div.head: The Eagle
div.p: Of the eagle, David says in the hundred and second psalm: 'Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's.'

The Physiologus says the eagle has this nature: when it grows old, its wings become heavy, and its eyes are covered with a dimness; then it seeks a spring of water, and flies up over that spring into the height, up to the sun's own air, and there it burns its wings, and burns away the dimness of its eyes with the sun's ray; then at last, descending to the spring, it plunges itself in three times, and is at once wholly renewed, so that it is renewed far better both in the vigor of its wings and in the brightness of its eyes.

So you too, man, whether Jew or Gentile, who wear the old garment, and whose heart's eyes are dimmed, seek the spiritual fountain of the Lord, who said: 'Unless a man is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God's heaven.' Unless, then, you are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and lift up the eyes of your heart to the Lord, who is the sun of righteousness, your youth shall not be renewed like the eagle's.

div.head: The Phoenix
div.p: There is another bird called the phoenix; our Lord Jesus Christ bears the likeness of it, he who says in his Gospel: 'I have power to lay down my life, and to take it again.' Because of these words the Jews were angered, and wished to stone him.

There is, then, a bird in the regions of India called the phoenix; of it the Physiologus says that, when five hundred years of its life are completed, it enters into the trees of Lebanon and fills both its wings with various spices; and by certain signs this is made known to the priest of the city of Heliopolis, that is, in the ninth month, Nisan or Adar, that is, Pharmuthi or Phamenoth, which is the month of March or April; and when this has been made known to the priest, he enters and fills the altar with sarment-wood. And when the bird arrives, it enters the city of Heliopolis, laden with all manner of spices in both its wings; and seeing at once the pile of wood made ready upon the altar, it mounts up; and, wrapping itself in the spices, itself kindles the fire and burns itself up. On another day the priest comes, and, seeing the wood consumed which he had laid upon the altar, searching, finds there a small worm smelling most sweetly. On the second day he finds it already shaped into a little bird. Again on the third day, the priest coming, finds it whole and perfect in its own form, the phoenix bird. And bidding the priest farewell, it flies up and returns to its former place.

If then this bird has the power to put itself to death and again to bring itself to life, how do foolish men grow angry at the word of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, as true man and true Son of God, had power to lay down his life and to take it again. So then, as we have already said, he takes on the person of our Savior, who, descending from heaven, filled both his wings with the sweetest fragrances, that is, the words of the New and Old Testament, saying: 'I have not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill it.' And again: 'Thus shall every scribe who is learned in the kingdom of heaven be, who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.'

div.head: The Hoopoe
div.p: It is said in the law: 'Honor your father and your mother'; and again: 'Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die.'

The Physiologus says: there is a bird called the hoopoe; when its young see that their parents have grown old, and can neither fly nor see, for the dimness of their eyes, then the young pluck out the aged feathers of their parents, and lick their parents' eyes, and warm them beneath their own wings, until their feathers grow back and their eyes are lit again, so that their whole body may be renewed as before, and they may see and fly. And afterward the parents give thanks to their children, who have shown them such dutiful care; and their children say to them: 'Behold, sweetest parents, just as you raised us from infancy, and spent all your labor upon us, we now render to you the same services of devotion in your old age.'
If irrational birds do this for one another, how is it that men, though rational, are unwilling to repay the nurture of their parents?

div.head: The Ant
div.p: Of the ant, Solomon says: 'Go to the ant, O sluggard, consider her; who, though weaker in strength, lays up much grain for herself in summer.'
The Physiologus says the ant has three natures.

Its first nature is this: when they go out of their den, they walk in order, and seek grains of any seed; and when they find one, each seizes a single grain with its mouth, carrying it to its den. But other ants not having grain in their mouth, though empty, do not say to those carrying food in their mouths: 'Give us of your store'; but they go seeking along their tracks, and take just as those did, and carry it to their own dwellings.

These things indeed are said of irrational animals and lowly creeping things, that they act so prudently that not one of them is found foolish, but all are found shrewd and wise: how much more ought those five foolish virgins, who through their own negligence became foolish -- though rational -- to have imitated the five wise ones, and taken oil in their own vessels, whence those others had taken it, rather than through idleness and folly asking of the wise, saying: 'Give us of your oil.' O such foolish folly! For if they could not understand this of themselves, they ought at least to have obtained it whence the others obtained it, or to have imitated the diligence of the ants. But while hoping for oil from others' vessels, when the bridegroom came, they were left outside, foolish, with their lamps extinguished.
Its second nature is: when it stores grain in its den, it divides it in half, lest, soaked in winter, the seed brought in should sprout.

And you, man of God, divide the scripture of the Old Testament into two parts, that is, according to its history and according to its spiritual meaning; divide the truth from the figure, separate spiritual things from bodily things, pass over from the letter that kills to the spirit that gives life, lest, the letter sprouting on the day of winter -- that is, on the day of judgment -- you perish of hunger. For the Apostle says: 'The law is spiritual, not carnal'; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life; and elsewhere: 'These things happened to them as a figure, but were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.' For the Jews, following the letter and despising the spiritual meaning, became the killers of the prophets and the murderers of their own Lord. And therefore even now they perish of hunger, because, occupied with empty chaff, they have lost the wheat. But you, man of God, strip the branches and remove their bark, as Jacob did; and put them into the waters, that your sheep may bring forth pure and spiritual fruits, and not carnal and vicious offspring. But all these things are intelligible to those who believe spiritually, and unintelligible to those who do not believe.

Its third nature is: at harvest time, among the crops, it knows by scent whether an ear is barley or wheat. If it is barley, it passes on to another ear and smells it; and when it perceives that the ear is wheat, it climbs up upon it, and, taking a grain from it, brings it down and carries it to its dwelling. For barley is the food of dumb animals; hence Job says: 'Instead of wheat, let thistles grow for me' -- rather, 'let barley spring up for me instead of wheat.'

Flee, then, man of God, from barley, that is, from the teaching of heretics: for they are of barley, and are to be cast away like rocks that shatter; and heresies destroy the souls of men; flee therefore Sabellius, Marcion, Mani; beware Novatian, Montanus, Valentinus, Basilides, Macedonius; beware Donatus and Photinus, and all who spring from the Arian stock, as offspring from the womb of the serpent-dragon: the teachings of these men are false and hostile to the truth.

div.head: The Sirens and the Onocentaurs
div.p: The prophet Isaiah says: 'Sirens and demons shall dance in Babylon, and hedgehogs and onocentaurs shall dwell in their houses.'

The Physiologus discusses the nature of each: sirens, he says, are deadly creatures; from the head to the navel they have the shape of a human being, but the remaining part, down to the feet, has the shape of a bird; and they sing a certain musical and most sweet melody, so that by the sweetness of their voice they beguile the hearing of men sailing from afar and draw them to themselves, and by the excessive sweetness of their prolonged song, lulling their ears and senses, turn them to sleep. Then, when they see them sunk in the deepest sleep, they set upon them and tear their flesh apart, and thus, through the persuasion of their voice, deceive unwitting and foolish men and put them to death for themselves. So too, then, are those deceived who delight in the pleasures of this world, and in its pomps and theatrical delights, dissolved by tragedies and various musical melodies, and, as though weighed down and lulled to sleep, become the prey of the Adversary.
The Physiologus affirms that the onocentaur consists of two natures, that is: the upper part is like a man, but the members of the lower part are of a wholly wild nature.

To this are likened senseless and double-tongued, deformed men; as the Apostle says: 'having the appearance of godliness but denying its power.' The prophet David says: 'Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he is compared to the senseless beasts, and made like them.'

div.head: The Hedgehog
div.p: The Physiologus says the hedgehog has the shape of a suckling piglet. On the outside it is entirely covered with spines; but at the time of the grape harvest it enters the vineyard, and where it sees a good cluster of grapes, it climbs up onto the vine, and strips the grapes from the cluster, so that all the berries fall to the ground; then it comes down and rolls itself over them, so that all the berries stick fast to its spines; and thus it carries food to its young.

But you, man of God, guard diligently your vineyard and all its spiritual fruits, lest the cares of this world and the pleasure of temporal goods take hold of you; for then the spiny devil, scattering all your spiritual fruits, will fix them upon his own spines and make you food for the beasts, and your soul will become naked, empty, and void, like a vine-branch without fruit; and afterward you will cry out in vain, saying: 'I did not guard my own vineyard,' as Scripture testifies in the Song of Songs.
Fittingly, then, has the Physiologus brought together the natures of animals and woven them into the understanding of the spiritual scriptures.

div.head: The Ibis
div.p: There is a bird called the ibis; this, according to the law, is unclean above all birds, since it always feeds on dead carcasses, and walks by day and by night along the shores of the sea, or rivers, or pools, seeking either dead little fish or some carcass that has been cast ashore, already rotten or decaying from the water. For it fears to enter the water, because it does not know how to swim; nor does it trouble to learn, since it delights in dead carcasses. Therefore it cannot go into the depths of the water where the clean little fish stay, to catch its food there; but it always wanders about outside, avoiding the purer and deeper waters, whence a clean creature might live.

You, then, Christian man, who have already been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, enter into intelligible and spiritual waters, that is, into the depth of the ministers of Christ; and from there take for yourself spiritual and most pure food, which the Apostle enumerates, saying: 'The fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity.' But if you are unwilling to enter into deeper waters, and to take and receive spiritual food from them, but instead, wandering about outside, are fattened on dead and most foul carcasses -- of which the Apostle says: 'Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are uncleanness, adulteries, fornication, immodesty, luxury, idolatry, drunkenness, avarice, covetousness' -- these are the fleshly and deadly foods on which unhappy souls are nourished unto punishment. Learn, then, to swim upon: 'This great and wide sea, wherein are creeping things without number,' with your own hands; nor can you overcome them otherwise than by the sign of the cross; and when you pray, stretch out your hands to heaven, for the power of the cross always defends those who pray and say: 'The light of your countenance is signed upon us, O Lord.' For the sun itself, unless it extends its rays, does not shine; the moon, unless it puts forth its horns, does not shine; birds, unless they spread their wings, cannot fly; ships, unless they raise their sails, will not be moved though the wind blows. Indeed, while Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; when he let his hands fall, Amalek grew strong. So then all the saints are figured in this: like birds passing over, they reach the kingdom of heaven as a most quiet harbor; but those who do not know how to swim spiritually, but are occupied with earthly and mortal works, are shut out from the kingdom of heaven, and perish, dead among the dead; as the Lord says in his Gospel: 'Let the dead bury their own dead.'
Fittingly, then, does the Physiologus speak.

div.head: The Fox
div.p: The fox is a deceitful and most fraudulent and cunning animal. When it is hungry and finds nothing to eat, it seeks out a place where the earth is red, and rolls itself over it, so that it appears entirely as if bloodied; and it throws itself upon the ground, and rolls upon it as though dead; and, drawing its breath within itself, it swells itself up so that it seems not to breathe at all. Birds, seeing it lying thus swollen and as if bloodied, with its tongue hanging out of its open mouth, think it is dead; and they come down and perch upon it: but it seizes them and devours them.

The fox, then, has the likeness of the devil: to all who live according to the flesh, he pretends to be dead; though within his throat he holds sinners, yet to the spiritual and those perfect in faith, he is truly dead and reduced to nothing. But those who wish to practice his works desire to be fattened on his flesh -- that is, the devil's -- which are: adulteries, fornications, idolatry, sorceries, murders, thefts, false witness, and other things like these; as the Apostle says: 'Knowing this, that if you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live.' Those, then, who live according to the flesh, occupied with the devil's works, are held bound to him, and, made his equals, shall perish together with him; as David says: 'They shall enter the depths of the earth, they shall be given over to the power of the sword, they shall be the portion of foxes.' Indeed Herod too was likened to the crafty fox, the Lord saying: 'Go, tell that fox'; and elsewhere the scribe, hearing from the Savior: 'Foxes have holes.' And in the Song of Songs: 'Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.'
Well, then, has the Physiologus spoken of the fox.

div.head: The Unicorn
div.p: There is an animal called in Greek 'monoceros,' in Latin 'unicornis.' The Physiologus says the unicorn has this nature: it is a small animal, like a kid, exceedingly fierce, having one horn in the middle of its head. No hunter at all can capture it; but by this device they catch it: they lead a virgin maiden to the place where it dwells, and leave her alone in the woods; and the animal, as soon as it sees her, leaps into the virgin's lap, and embraces her, and is thus captured, and is displayed in the palace of the king.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ, the spiritual unicorn, descending into the womb of the virgin through the flesh taken from her, was captured by the Jews, and condemned to death on the cross; of whom David says: 'And beloved as the son of unicorns'; and again in another psalm he himself says of himself: 'And my horn shall be exalted like the unicorn's.' And Zechariah says: 'He has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant.' And in Deuteronomy, Moses, blessing the tribe of Joseph: 'His glory is like the firstborn of a bull, his horns are like the horns of the unicorn.' That it has one horn on its head signifies what the Savior says: 'I and the Father are one.' For the head of Christ is God, according to the Apostle. That it is called exceedingly fierce means that neither principalities nor powers, neither thrones nor dominions could understand it, nor could hell hold it fast. That it is called a small animal is because of the humility of his incarnation; as he himself says: 'Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly of heart.' Yet so fierce that not even the most subtle devil could understand or discover it, but by the will of the Father alone he descended into the womb of the Virgin Mary for our salvation:

And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. And that the unicorn is like a kid -- our Savior too, according to the Apostle, was made in the likeness of sinful flesh, and by sin he condemned sin in the flesh. Well, then, has it been said of the unicorn.

div.head: The Beaver
div.p: There is an animal called the beaver, exceedingly gentle, whose testicles are useful in medicine for various ailments. The Physiologus has set forth its nature, saying that when a hunter tracks it down and pursues it, the beaver, looking back and seeing the hunter coming after it, at once bites off its own testicles, and casts them before the hunter's face, and so escapes by flight; and the hunter, coming up, gathers them, and no longer pursues it further, but withdraws from it. But if it should happen again that another hunter, searching, finds and follows it, then, seeing that it can no longer escape, it rises up and shows the hunter its own body; and the hunter, seeing that it no longer has its testicles, departs from it.

So too everyone who lives according to God's commandment, and wishes to live chastely, cuts off from himself all vices and every act of unchastity, and casts them behind him before the face of the devil; then the devil, seeing him possessing nothing of his own, departs from him in confusion. He, then, lives in God and is not seized by the devil who says: 'I will pursue and overtake him.' The man of God, then, ought to have nothing of the devil's, so that, trusting in the Lord, he may boldly say: 'The prince of this world came, and found nothing in me.' For the Apostle admonishes us and says: 'Render to all their dues, tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honor to whom honor.' First, then, let there be rendered to the devil what is his, that is, renouncing him and all his evil works; then at last, turned to God with the whole heart, you will render him honor as to a father, and fear as to a lord. And separate yourself from the works of the flesh, which are the devil's due and tribute; and let us obtain the spiritual fruits, that is: love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, chastity, in good works -- that is, in almsgiving, in visiting the sick, in caring for the poor, in the praises of God, in prayers, in giving thanks, and in the other things that are God's.

div.head: The Hyena
div.p: There is an animal called in Greek 'hyaena,' in Latin 'belua,' of which the law says: 'You shall not eat the hyena, nor anything like it, for it is unclean.' Of it, too, it is said through the prophet Jeremiah: 'The den of the hyena has become my inheritance.'
The Physiologus says of it that the hyena has two natures: sometimes it is male, sometimes female, and therefore it is an unclean animal.

To it the sons of Israel are likened, since from the beginning they served the living God, but afterward, given over to pleasures and luxury, they worshipped idols. For this reason the prophet compared the synagogue to this unclean animal. But also whoever among us, devoted to pleasure and avarice -- according to the Apostle: 'the root of all evils is the service of idols' -- are likened to this same unclean beast, since they are neither men nor women, that is, neither faithful nor unfaithful, but without doubt something in between; of whom Solomon says: 'A man of double mind is inconstant in all his ways.' And the Savior says to them in the Gospel: 'You cannot serve two masters,' that is, God and Mammon.

div.head: The Hydrus
div.p: There is another animal in the river Nile, called the hydrus. The Physiologus says of it that this animal is quite hostile to the crocodile. And it has this nature and custom: when it sees the crocodile sleeping on the riverbank with its mouth open, it goes and rolls itself in the mud, so that it may more easily slip into its jaws, and coming, leaps into its mouth; the crocodile, taken by surprise, swallows it alive; but the hydrus, tearing apart all its inward parts, comes out alive from the belly of the now-dead crocodile, all its innards having been torn asunder.

So then death and hell bear the likeness of the crocodile, which is the enemy of our Lord and Savior; and therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, taking on our earthly flesh, descended into hell and, tearing apart all its inward parts, led out all who were held captive in death, devoured by it; as the Evangelist testifies: 'And the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints arose.' He put death itself to death; and he himself, living, rose from the dead, and mocks it, saying through the prophet: 'O death, I will be your death; I will be your bite, O hell.' And elsewhere: 'Death is swallowed up in the victory of Christ; where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your destruction?'

div.head: The Roe Deer
div.p: There is an animal called in Greek 'dorcon,' in Latin 'caprea.' Of it the Physiologus says that it loves high mountains, but feeds in the valleys of the mountains. It is a keenly perceptive animal, seeing very far into the distance, so that if it suddenly sees men walking in another region, it at once recognizes whether they are hunters or travelers.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ loves the high mountains, that is, the prophets and apostles and patriarchs; as he says in the Song of Songs: 'Behold, my beloved comes like a roe, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.' And as the roe feeds in the valleys, so our Lord Jesus Christ feeds in the Church, since the good works of Christians and the alms of the faithful are Christ's food -- he who said: 'I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink,' and the rest that follows. The valleys of the mountains, which are throughout the whole world, are understood as the churches in their various places; as it says in the Song of Songs: 'Return, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of the valleys.' And since the roe has the keenest sight of eyes, and sees all things from afar and knows them from a distance, this signifies our Savior; as Scripture says: 'The Lord is a God of knowledge.' And in psalm one hundred thirty-seven: 'The Lord is high, and regards the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar.' And all things that are, his divine majesty has created and established and rules and sees and looks upon, and before anything arises in our hearts, in word, deed, or thought, God already foresees and knows it from afar. Just, then, as the roe knows from afar the tricks of hunters, so our Lord Jesus Christ foresaw and foreknew the tricks of the devil and the snares of his betrayer Judas; and indeed he said to Judas: 'With a kiss you betray the Son of man.'
Well, then, has the Physiologus explained concerning the roe.

div.head: The Wild Ass and the Ape
div.p: There is another animal called the wild ass. The Physiologus says of the wild ass that on the twenty-fifth day of the month Phamenoth, which is March, it brays twelve times in the night, and likewise in the day; and from this it is known that it is the equinox of day or night, and men know the number of the hours by each single bray of the wild ass.

The wild ass, then, has the likeness of the devil, because it knows when night and day become equal (that is, when the devil sees that the people who walk in darkness and the shadow of death are now turning to the living Lord, and are being made equal to the faith of the patriarchs and prophets, just as night is made equal with day); therefore he roars by day and by night, at every hour, seeking the food he has lost. For the wild ass does not bray except when it seeks its food -- as Job says: 'Does the wild ass bray without cause, unless it desires pasture?' Likewise the apostle Peter says of the devil: 'Our adversary goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.' Likewise the ape too has the likeness of the devil: for as the ape has indeed a head, but has no tail, and although it is entirely ugly, yet its hindparts are especially ugly and repellent; so too the devil indeed had a head, but had no tail: that is, he had a beginning, when he was an angel in heaven, but because he was a hypocrite and deceitful within, he lost his head; nor does he have a tail, that is, just as he perished from the beginning in heaven, so at the end he shall wholly perish -- as Paul, the herald of truth, says: 'whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the breath of his mouth.'

div.head: The Coot
div.p: There is a bird called the coot, quite intelligent and most prudent above all birds. It does not feed on carrion, nor does it fly here and there, wandering about, but remains and stays in one place until the end, and there has its food, and there rests; as David says: 'The coot's house is their leader.'

So then every faithful man is kept and lives according to God's will; he does not fly here and there through various places, as heretics do; nor does he delight in worldly desires and bodily pleasures, as do those birds that feed on flesh; but he always keeps and rests in one and the same place, that is, in the catholic and apostolic church, and there remains until the end; as the Lord says in the Gospel: 'He who perseveres to the end shall be saved.' There, then, he keeps himself, where the Lord: 'makes those of one mind to dwell in a house'; and there he has the daily bread of immortality, and for his drink the precious blood of Christ, refreshing himself with holy banquets and, above honey and the honeycomb, with the sweetest words of the Lord: 'For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.'

div.head: The Panther
div.p: There is an animal called the panther, of varied color indeed, but exceedingly beautiful, and most gentle. The Physiologus says of it that it has only one enemy, the dragon. When it has eaten and satisfied itself with various prey, it retires into its den, lies down, and sleeps; after three days it rises from sleep, and at once lets out a great roar; and together with the roar, a fragrance of sweetness comes forth from its mouth, so that it surpasses all spices. When, then, all the beasts, both near and far, hear its voice, they all gather together and follow the sweetness of the fragrance that comes from its mouth; only the dragon, when it hears its voice, shrinks back in fear, and hides itself in the caverns of the earth, unable to bear the force of the sweet fragrance there: contracted into itself, it grows numb, and remains there motionless and empty as though dead; but the other animals follow the panther wherever it goes.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ, the true panther, drawing to himself through his incarnation all mankind (which had been captured by the devil and held liable to death), 'led captivity captive,' as David the prophet says: 'Ascending on high, you began to lead captivity, you received gifts among men.' For the panther is interpreted as 'catching all things': just as our Lord God (as we have said), seeing mankind captured by demons and enslaved to idols, and all nations and peoples made the devil's prey, descending from the heavens, snatched us from the power of the devil, and joined us to his own goodness; and he brought us as children into the fatherly love, and fulfilled what the prophet had foretold before: 'I,' he says, 'have become like a panther to Ephraim, and like a lion to the house of Judah, who served idols.' By this he signified then the calling of the Gentiles and the Jews. And the panther is a varied animal, as it is said through Solomon of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the wisdom of God -- a spirit intelligible, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, mobile, sure, uncontaminated, true, sweet, loving the good, keen, hindering no good from being done, merciful, firm, stable, secure, all-powerful, all-seeing, all-doing, more mobile than all wisdom, and the rest. That Christ is the divine wisdom, the teacher of truth, Paul, testifies, saying: 'But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, to the Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, both Jews and Gentiles, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.' And because the panther is a beautiful animal, David says of Christ: 'Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.' And because it is an exceedingly gentle animal, Isaiah says: 'Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem, for your king comes to you, gentle and bringing salvation.' And because, when it has eaten and is satisfied, it immediately rests and sleeps, so too our Lord Jesus Christ, after he was sated with the mockeries of the Jews -- that is, with scourgings, blows, insults, reproaches, thorns, spittings -- his hands nailed and hung upon the cross, given gall and vinegar to drink, and pierced besides with a spear: sated, then, with so many and such great gifts of the Jews, Christ fell asleep and rested in the tomb and descended into hell, and there bound the great dragon, our enemy. And that on the third day that animal rises from sleep and lets out a great roar and a fragrance of sweetness breathes from its mouth -- so too our Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead on the third day, as the Psalmist says: 'The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man flushed with wine.' And at once he cried out with a great voice, so that his sound went out into all the earth, and his words to the ends of the world, saying: 'Rejoice, and do not be afraid, for I have overcome the world'; and again: 'Holy Father, those you gave me I have kept, and none of them is lost but the son of perdition'; and again: 'I go to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God'; and again: 'I will come to you, and will not leave you orphans.' And at the end of the Gospel he says: 'Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.' And just as from the panther's mouth comes a fragrance of sweetness, and all who are near and who are far off (that is, the Jews, who once had the perception of beasts, who were near through the law; and the Gentiles, who were far off, without the law), hearing his voice, filled and refreshed by the most sweet fragrance of his commandments, follow him, crying out with the prophet and saying: 'How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.' Of these fragrances of his commandments David says: 'Grace is poured out upon your lips, therefore God has blessed you forever.' And Solomon in the Song of Songs says of him: 'The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.' For what else can the ointments of Christ be, but his commandments, which are above all spices? For just as the presence of spices gives forth a fragrance of sweetness, so too the words of the Lord, which come forth from his mouth, gladden the hearts of men who hear and follow him. 'Your name is poured-out ointment, therefore the young maidens have loved you'; and: 'They have drawn you after them, and we run to the fragrance of your ointments'; and a little after: 'The king has brought me into his chamber.' We ought, then, as quickly as possible, like young maidens -- that is, souls renewed in baptism -- to run after the ointments of Christ's commandments, to pass over from earthly things to heavenly, so that the king may bring us into his palace, that is, into Jerusalem, the city of God, and into the mountain of all the saints; and when we have been found worthy to enter there, let us say: 'Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God'; as we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts.
Well, then, has the Physiologus spoken of the panther.

div.head: The Aspidochelone
div.p: There is a sea-monster called in Greek 'aspidochelone,' in Latin 'aspido-turtle';

it is, then, a great whale, having upon its hide something like sandy shoals, as along the shores of the sea. This creature, in the middle of the open sea, raises its back up above the waves of the sea, so that sailing men believe it to be nothing other than an island, especially when they see that whole place covered with sand, as on all the shores of the sea. Thinking it to be an island, they moor their ship beside it, and, disembarking, drive in stakes and tie up their ships; then, to cook their food after their labor, they make fires there upon the sand as though upon the ground; but that beast, when it feels the heat of the fire, suddenly plunges into the water, and drags the ship with it into the depths of the sea.

So it happens to all who are unbelieving and ignorant of the devil's cunning, placing their hope in him; and, binding themselves to his works, are plunged together with him into the fire of burning hell: such is his cunning.

The second nature of this monster is this: when it is hungry, it opens its mouth, and breathes out from its mouth a kind of sweet-smelling scent; and as soon as the smaller fish perceive its fragrance, they gather themselves within its mouth; and when its mouth is filled with various small fish, it suddenly closes its mouth and swallows them.

So it happens to all who are of little faith, who, enticed by pleasures and allurements as if by certain devilish fragrances, are suddenly swallowed up by him like tiny fish; for the greater ones keep themselves from him and do not even come near him. So then those who always keep Christ in their mind are great in his sight; and if they are perfect, they recognize the manifold wiles of the devil, and guard themselves against him and resist him all the more: and he flees from them. But doubtful men, and men of little faith, while they go after the pleasures and luxuries of the devil, are deceived; as Scripture says: 'They delight in ointments and various perfumes, and so the soul is broken by ruin.'

div.head: The Partridge
div.p: There is a bird called the partridge, exceedingly deceitful, as the holy prophet Jeremiah says of it: 'The partridge has cried out, and gathered what she did not hatch, making herself riches unjustly; in the midst of her days they shall forsake her, and in her latter end she shall be a fool.'

The Physiologus says the partridge is quite cunning, in that she steals the eggs of another -- that is, of another partridge -- and warms them with her own body; but she cannot enjoy the fruit of her fraud, because, once she has raised the stolen chicks, she loses them; for as soon as they hear the voice of their true mother, who laid the eggs, they at once fly off and betake themselves to their natural parents; and thus, having gained a certain reward and abandoned the love, she who poured out her labors in vain upon another's young, is punished for her fraud, and remains foolish and alone and empty.

The devil is an imitator of this bird, who strives to steal away the offspring of the eternal Creator; and if he can in some way gather together any who are foolish and lack the vigor of their own senses, he cherishes them with bodily allurements; but when the voice of Christ is heard by these little ones, taking to themselves spiritual wings through faith, they fly off and commend themselves to Christ, who at once receives them beneath the shadow of his wings with a certain most fatherly gift and love, and gives them to be nurtured by mother Church.

div.head: The Weasel and the Asp
div.p: The law commands that the weasel not be eaten, because it is an unclean animal.
The Physiologus says that the weasel receives the male's seed through the mouth, and so carries it in the womb; but at the time of giving birth, she brings it forth through the ears.
So are some among the faithful: they gladly receive the seed of the divine word, but, having become disobedient, they set it aside and disregard what they have heard.

Such as these are compared not only to the weasel, but also to the deaf asp, which stops her ears and does not hear the voice of the charmer. The Physiologus says the asp has this nature: when some man comes to the cave where the asp dwells, and charms it with all his incantations to make it come out of its lair, the asp, so as not to hear the voice of the charmer, puts its head to the ground, and presses one ear into the earth, while it stops the other ear with its tail. Such are the rich men of this world, who press down one ear into earthly desires; and the other, ever adding new sins to their former sins, they stop up; and so it comes about that they do not hear the voice of the charmer, that is, the preachers. And this indeed is the only thing asps do -- they stop their ears. But these men also blind their eyes with earthly desires and plunder, so that they are unwilling either to hear and keep the divine commandments with their ears, or to look up to heaven with their eyes and think of him who is above the heavens, and who does good and justice. Those who now refuse to hear God through preachers and the divine scriptures shall hear him on the day of judgment, saying: 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.'

div.head: The Ostrich
div.p: Likewise there is an animal called 'asida,' which the Greeks call 'struthiocamelon,' the Latins 'struthio.' Of this animal the prophet Jeremiah says: 'And the asida in the sky knows her time.'

The Physiologus says this is somewhat like a vulture; it has feathers indeed, but does not fly like the other birds; it has feet like a camel, and therefore in Greek is called 'struthiocamelon.' This animal, then, when the time comes for it to lay its eggs, lifts its eyes to heaven and watches whether that star called the Pleiades has risen; for it does not lay its eggs on the ground except when that star rises in the sky. Of this star Job says: 'He who made the Pleiades and Orion, and the chambers of the south.' For in its own season the star Pleiades rises in the sky, that is, when the harvests flower and it is summer, around the month of June; then the ostrich, when it has seen the Pleiades ascend into the sky, digs in the earth and there lays its eggs, and covers them with sand in the wilderness; and when it has risen from that place, it at once forgets and does not return to its eggs. For this animal is by nature forgetful; and so, in the season of summer, it lays its eggs and buries them in the sand, so that what it would otherwise have done -- sitting upon its eggs and, from its own brooding, bringing forth its chicks -- the calm of the season and the mildness of the air seem to provide for it instead, so that in summer the heated sand cooks the eggs and hatches out those chicks.

If, then, the ostrich knows its own season and lifts its eyes to heaven, and forgets its own offspring, how much more ought we to know our own season, to forget earthly things and follow heavenly ones, and to lift up the eyes of our heart? As the Apostle says: 'Forgetting what is behind, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly calling.' And the Lord says in the Gospel: 'He who loves father or mother or children more than me is not worthy of me.' And to him who excused himself on account of his father's burial he says: 'Let the dead bury their own dead, but you, come, follow me.'

div.head: The Turtledove
div.p: There is a bird called the turtledove; it is written of her: 'The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.'

The Physiologus says of the turtledove that she loves her mate exceedingly, and lives chastely with him, and keeps faith to him alone; so that if it should ever happen that her mate is caught either by a hawk or a fowler, she does not join herself to another mate, but always longs for him, and hopes for him at every moment, and perseveres, remembering and longing for him, even unto death.

Hear, then, all faithful souls, how great a chastity is found in so small a bird; whoever of you bear the likeness of the turtledove in the countenance of your soul, imitate her chastity. For such is the holy Church, which, after she saw her husband crucified, and rising on the third day, and ascending into heaven, does not join herself to another husband, but longs for him and hopes for him, and perseveres in love and devotion to him even unto death; as our Lord Jesus Christ says: 'He who perseveres to the end shall be saved.' Likewise the prophet David also exhorts, saying in the psalm: 'Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord.'

div.head: The Stag
div.p: Likewise in the forty-first psalm: 'As the stag longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.'

The Physiologus says that when the stag knows there is a serpent, it fills its mouth with water and pours it into the serpent's hole, and with a certain breath of its mouth draws the serpent out, and, trampling it with its feet, kills it.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ, seeing the enemy, the devil, dwelling in a certain den within every nation of mankind, having within himself the fountain of divine wisdom, whose words the ancient dragon cannot bear. For when he had been seen in the region of the Gerasenes, that dragon rushed forth of his own accord, along with all the host of demons dwelling within a single man, and said: 'What have I to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?'; and the Lord asked him: 'What is your name?' and he answered: 'My name is Legion.' And they begged Jesus not to command them to go into the abyss. Now there was a herd of many swine feeding there; and the demons begged him, saying: 'If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine'; and Jesus said to them: 'Go'; and they, going out from the men, entered into the swine; and behold, the whole herd rushed with great violence down the steep bank into the sea, about two thousand, and were drowned in the waters. Behold how, hearing the voice of the Lord, the devil fled headlong with all his followers; of whom in the last days the Apostle testifies, saying: 'whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the breath of his mouth.' And David says: 'The high mountains are for the stags.' By the mountains he means the apostles and prophets, and by the stags, the faithful, who through the apostles and prophets and priests come to the knowledge of Christ; as it is written in the psalm: 'I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence shall come my help.'

div.head: The Salamander
div.p: There is a certain reptile called in Greek 'salamandra,' in Latin 'stellio'; this is like a small lizard, of varied color; of which Solomon says: 'Like the stellio, dwelling in the houses of kings.' The Physiologus says of it that if by chance it falls into a furnace of fire, or into a burning oven, or into any fire whatsoever, the fire is at once extinguished.

Such are the righteous and wonderful men of God; as were Ananias, Azarias, and Misael in the furnace of burning fire, whom the fire did not touch at all, as the prophet Daniel clearly declares, that they came out of the furnace untouched and unharmed. And the apostle Paul testifies, saying: 'By faith all the saints extinguished the power of fire, stopped the mouths of lions.' So too everyone who believes with his whole faith in God and perseveres in good works passes through the fire of hell, and the flame does not touch him; of whom it is written in the prophet Isaiah: 'If you pass through the fire, the flame shall not burn you.'

div.head: The Doves
div.p: The Physiologus says that doves are of many and varied colors, that is, starling-colored, black, white, crowned, spotted, sky-colored, ashen, golden, honey-colored; but the red is chief above them all, who rules and calms them all, and daily gathers even the wild ones into his own dovecote.

He, then, is the first, who redeemed us with his precious blood, and gathered us together within the one house of the Church from among the various nations; not Moses, not Elijah, not any of the prophets or patriarchs, but he himself, coming from the Father, saved us, and through his own passion redeemed us from eternal death; as John says: 'I saw heaven opened, and the Spirit of God descending like a dove,' sent by God, who wishes 'all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.' He, then, wishing to gather mankind into the holy catholic and apostolic church, sent the Holy Spirit, 'speaking in many portions and in many ways' through the law and the prophets to all mankind, just as the coloring of doves is varied. The first color signifies the law, being as it were black, that is, because of the obscure sayings and the meaning that requires interpretation. Then the starling color signifies the diversity of the twelve prophets. The sky color signifies Elijah, who was caught up through the air in a chariot even to heaven. The ashen color signifies the prophet Jonah, preaching to the Ninevites that they should do penance in sackcloth and ashes, by which act the safeguard of life was granted him by the Lord. The golden color signifies none other than the three youths, who, having the true spirit of God, said to King Nebuchadnezzar: 'Know, O king, that we do not worship your gods, nor will we adore the golden image which you have set up.' The honey color is Elisha, who received the mantle from his master Elijah as he went up into heaven, and was found worthy to be honored with a double portion of his spirit. The white color is the blessed John, the forerunner of Christ, having the whiteness of holy baptism; of whom the prophet Isaiah says: 'Wash yourselves, be clean, take away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes, learn to do good'; and: 'though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow.' Of John the Lord testifies, saying: 'Amen I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen a greater than John the Baptist.' For the law and the prophets prophesied until John, but he pointed out Christ with his finger: 'Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.' The crowned color is Stephen, the first martyr, who, after receiving the Holy Spirit, was found worthy to see Christ at the right hand of the Father. The red color signifies the Lord's passion, on account of which the harlot Rahab even then sent forth the scarlet sign, by which she was saved in Jericho; of which it is said in the Song of Songs: 'Your lips are like a scarlet thread.' And in the Gospel it says: 'The Jews put upon the Lord a scarlet robe.' And Isaiah says: 'Who is this who comes from Edom, his garment red from Bozrah?' And a scarlet thread was bound upon the hand of Zerah, son of Judah, by the midwife, while he was yet in his mother's womb. And in the Song of Songs: 'My beloved is white and ruddy' -- white in virginity, ruddy in martyrdom, through which all who believe in him have been redeemed by his precious blood, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is blessed forever and ever, Amen.

div.head: The Peredixion Tree
div.p: Likewise another thing is told concerning these same doves: there is a certain tree in the regions of India, called in Greek 'peredixion,' in Latin 'circa dexteram' (that is, 'around the right hand'); whose fruit is exceedingly sweet, and most pleasant. Doves take great delight in the grace of this tree, since they are refreshed by its fruit, and rest beneath its shadow, and are sheltered by its branches. Now the dragon is a cruel enemy of the doves; and just as much as the doves fear the dragon and flee from him, so much does that dragon avoid and dread that tree, so that he does not even dare to come near its shadow. But while that dragon lies in wait for the doves, to snatch one of them, he watches that tree from afar; if the shadow of the tree is on the right side, he places himself on the left; but if its shadow is on the left, he, fleeing, places himself on the right. The doves, however, knowing that their enemy the dragon fears that tree and its shadow, and cannot come near it even slightly, therefore take refuge in that tree and commend themselves there, that they may be kept safe from the snares of their adversary. As long, then, as they remain in that tree and keep themselves within it, the dragon can in no way seize them; but if he finds one of them even slightly separated from the tree, or outside its shadow, he at once seizes and devours it. And these things the Physiologus relates concerning the doves.

We, then, Christians, knowing the tree (which is the peredixion), around which all is on the right hand, and nothing on it is on the left; its right hand is the only-begotten Son of God, as the Lord himself says: 'For the tree is known by its fruit.' The shadow of the tree is the Holy Spirit, as Gabriel says to holy Mary: 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.' The doves are all the faithful, as the Lord says in the Gospel: 'Be therefore simple as doves, and wise as serpents.' Be simple, so that you plot deceit against no one; and wise, so that you are not undermined by others' snares. Give heed to yourself always, then, man of God, and remain in the catholic faith, and there hold yourself, there dwell, there abide, there persevere in the one faith of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and in the one catholic Church; as the Psalmist says: 'Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity'; and elsewhere: 'who makes those of one mind to dwell in a house.' Beware, then, as much as you can, lest you be found outside this house, and that ancient serpent-dragon seize you and devour you, as he devoured Judas, who, as soon as he went out from the Lord and from his brother apostles, was at once devoured by the devil and perished.

div.head: The Elephant
div.p: There is an animal called the elephant. The Physiologus says of it that it has a great understanding within itself, but has scarcely any desire for mating. For in its own season, when it wishes to beget offspring, it goes eastward with its mate, as far as the nearest borders of paradise; and there is a tree there called the mandrake; and so the female first tastes of the fruit of that tree, and then entices the male, so that, persuaded, he too eats. And after both have eaten, then they come together with one another, and at once the female conceives in her womb; and when the time comes for her to give birth, she goes to where there is a pool of water, and enters the water up to her udders, and there gives birth upon the water, on account of the dragon, since he lies in wait for her; and if she gives birth outside the water, the dragon seizes and devours that offspring. Therefore she enters into the deep water, that she may give birth there; and her mate does not withdraw from her, but guards her as she gives birth, because of the serpent, which is the enemy of elephants.

These two elephants, then, male and female, bear the likeness of Adam and his wife Eve, who were in the paradise of God before their transgression, surrounded by glory, knowing no evil, no desire of concupiscence, no intercourse of mating; but when that woman tasted of the forbidden tree, she led her husband astray, and he too ate; then afterward, driven out of paradise, they were cast into this world, as though into a pool of many waters. Of which this world bears the likeness, because of its many fluctuations and interminglings, and its innumerable pleasures and passions; of which David says: 'Save me, O Lord, for the waters have come in even unto my soul'; and elsewhere: 'I waited patiently for the Lord, and he inclined to me, and heard my prayers, and brought me up out of the pit of misery and the mire of the depths.' Then Adam knew his wife, and begot Cain in the mire of the depths; and therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, descending as a merciful and compassionate one from the bosom of the Father, taking on our flesh, brought us up out of the pit of misery and the mire of the depths, and set our feet upon a rock, and put a new song into our mouths, a hymn to our God -- that is, when he taught us to pray -- then he put into our mouths a new song, saying: 'Thus shall you pray: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name,' and the rest. This hymn our own teacher taught us to offer to God, who set our feet upon a rock, and put a new song into our mouths, a hymn to our God. And this same thing the Apostle himself prays for us, saying: 'May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly, that your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.'

For the bones and hide of the elephant, wherever they are burned in any place or house, at once their scent drives out and puts to flight serpents from that place; or if there are any harmful venomous reptiles, they do not approach there. So too, then, the works or commandments of God, which a man carries within himself, purify his heart, and no thought of the Adversary can enter there; but whatever harmful and shameful thing might be there, at once departs and vanishes entirely, so that never does any harmful spirit or hostile thought, or any of its mischief, appear there again.
